title: Delegation can only be changed between proposals, so a continuous stream of live proposals leaves delegators locked in
content:
Two provisions combine into one constraint. A.6.1.1.2.3.1.4.2.2: "A snapshot records voting power at each proposal snapshot-block height. Voting power (including delegations) **cannot be altered for the duration of a specific active proposal**." A.6.1.1.2.3.1.4.2.3: "Delegators may revoke or move their delegation **whenever no proposal is live**. All changes take effect at the next snapshot-block."

The snapshot lock has a clear purpose. Without it, voting power could be acquired after a proposal's terms are known — borrowed, bought, or shuffled between wallets to vote twice. Fixing the electorate before the contest begins is what makes the vote meaningful.

The cost lands on delegators. A delegator who disagrees with how their delegate is voting on a live proposal has no remedy for that proposal: the power is already committed at the snapshot block, and revocation takes effect only at the next one. Accountability is entirely retrospective — you can fire your delegate, but only after they have cast the vote you objected to.

The non-obvious consequence is in the phrasing of the revocation window. Delegation may be changed "whenever no proposal is live," which makes the delegator's exit contingent on a *gap* in governance activity. Under a dense proposal schedule with overlapping voting windows, those gaps shrink, and in the limiting case of continuously live proposals they vanish — delegation becomes practically irrevocable without any rule saying so.

So governance throughput and delegator exit rights are coupled in a way neither provision mentions. A framework that responds to a busy period by running more proposals in parallel tightens the lock on every delegator at exactly the moment when the stakes of being locked in are highest.
description: Voting power is fixed at each proposal's snapshot block and delegators may revoke only when no proposal is live, making the delegator's remedy against a delegate's vote purely prospective.
